techniques need data and they need a lot of data. Data comes in two parts, the features as we call
which is the raw input, the images, the audio signals, your sensor data and then the labels.
Labels usually have to be provided by humans. So if you're for example trying to find all the
faces in the image then somebody needs to actually look at the image and draw little
bounding boxes around every face, so you know where they are. That is time consuming and also
very boring. So people don't like that. It's a job that needs to be done. Recently there has been
progress in a couple of techniques that make that a lot easier to do and they're called active learning
and cooperative learning which is a form of active learning. So the trick is quite simple
actually, it's working with the machine. So you have a little bit of data that you've collected
and part of that, let's say 10% of that you have annotated, painstakingly hours and hours of work
but you've got 10% of your data annotated. Now you can train a machine learner on that 10% of data
and then you can make predictions on the other 90% of data. Now you need a machine learner that gives
confidence on all its predictions so it doesn't just say there's a face, it has to say
I'm pretty sure there's a face there or I'm not so sure there might be a face but you know 10%
sure or something like that and what you can then do in active learning is you ask the human
to annotate the data that it's not sure about and then that way you only start annotating data
that it really needs to know about. So basically you have your database, let's say you start with
10%, you're going to train a machine learner on that, that gives you a hypothesis and that hypothesis
will take the other 90% of data that it hasn't been trained on yet and it makes predictions on that.
Now some of those predictions will have high confidence and you know those are probably not
